narrative:
The model estimates you have a 29% chance of failing your final year. While this is not a majority prediction, it is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to strengthen your preparation.

The three factors that most influenced this outlook were your number of past failures, the amount of free time you have after school, and your mother’s level of education. Past failures had the strongest effect and pushed the prediction toward passing because you have had none—matching the average of students who succeeded. However, this positive signal was outweighed by the other two features.

Your very low free time after school was the second most important factor and worked against you. Most students who pass report medium or high free time; your unusually low amount suggests you may be overloaded or struggling to balance demands, which the model associates with greater risk of failure.

Your mother’s primary education level was the third strongest influence and also nudged the outcome toward failing. Only 14% of students who pass have a mother educated only to primary level, so this background is relatively uncommon among successful students and appears to limit the academic support the model expects at home.

To improve, consider talking with a teacher or counselor about ways to create manageable study routines despite limited free time, and explore extra academic resources that can compensate for lower family educational background. Small, consistent steps in these areas can meaningfully raise your chances of passing.
